title: The Boys and the Frogs
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: Some mischievous Boys were playing on the edge of a pond, and, catching sight of some Frogs swimming about in the shallow water, they began to amuse themselves by pelting them with stones, and they killed several of them. At last one of the Frogs put his head out of the water and said, "Oh, stop! stop! I beg of you: what is sport to you is death to us."

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where are the Boys playing at the start?
options: Beside a river bridge
In a meadow near their homes
On the edge of a pond
Along a dusty road

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what do the Boys catch sight of in the shallow water?
options: Some Frogs swimming about
A school of small fish
A family of ducks
A turtle sunning itself

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how do the Boys amuse themselves?
options: By splashing water at each other
By racing along the pond's edge
By trying to catch the Frogs with their hands
By pelting the Frogs with stones

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what is the result of the Boys' game?
options: The Frogs all escaped unharmed
They killed several of the Frogs
The Boys grew tired and stopped quickly
The Frogs chased the Boys away

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Frog say when it puts its head out of the water?
options: "Please share your stones with us instead."
"We will leave this pond if you stop."
"What is sport to you is death to us."
"You will be punished for this someday."

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Frog beg the Boys to do?
options: Stop throwing the stones
Come closer to see them better
Return tomorrow with food instead
Move to a different pond

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why do the Boys likely see stone-throwing as harmless fun?
options: They believe the Frogs cannot actually be harmed by stones
They are trying to chase the Frogs to a safer pond
They think the Frogs enjoy the splashing water
They do not consider what the game means for the creatures being hit

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what point is the Frog making with its remark about "sport" and "death"?
options: Frogs are actually stronger than they appear to be
Something one side finds entertaining can be devastating for the other
The Boys should be playing a different game entirely
The pond is too shallow for the game to be fair

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "mischievous" mean in describing the Boys?
options: Extremely tired and sleepy
Careful and well-behaved
Inclined to cause playful trouble
Frightened of the water

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: What feels like harmless fun to one side can be a matter of life and death to another
Frogs should never swim near the edge of a pond
Boys are naturally crueler than other children
Games involving stones should always be supervised

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what were the Frogs doing before the Boys noticed them?
options: Resting on lily pads
Croaking loudly along the bank
Hiding beneath the surface
Swimming about in the shallow water

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which Frog is the one who finally speaks up?
options: The largest Frog in the pond
One of the Frogs, who puts his head out of the water
A Frog sitting safely on the bank
A Frog that had already been hit

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how many times does the Frog repeat the word "stop"?
options: Once
Three times
Twice
It does not say the word at all

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does it take until several Frogs are killed before one speaks up?
options: The Frogs have no way to communicate with the Boys until one is desperate enough to try
The Frogs are plotting a group escape before responding
The Boys ignore the Frogs' cries until this moment
The first Frog to speak is the leader of the group

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Frog's plea reveal about how differently the two sides experience the same act?
options: The Boys and Frogs actually want the same outcome
The Frogs enjoy the game as much as the Boys do
The stones cause no real harm to either side
The same action can be trivial for one side and devastating for the other

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "pelting" mean in "pelting them with stones"?
options: Gently placing something down
Throwing repeatedly at something
Collecting something from the ground
Sorting something into groups

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: Boys and Frogs play a game together at the pond
Frogs throw stones back at the Boys in retaliation
Boys throw stones at Frogs for fun until one Frog protests that it is deadly to them
Boys stop playing before any Frogs are harmed
